div.head: Norðleoda 6
div.ab: Ceorles wergild is CC ⁊ LXVI þrimsa, þæt bið II hund scill'. be Myrcna lage.
Ceorles wergyld is CC ⁊ VI ⁊ LX þrymsa, þæt bið twahund scyllinga be Myrcna lage.
Ceorles weregild biþ CCLXVII ðrimsa be ðam Dena laga.
Ceorles weregildum est CCLXVI þrimsa, id est CC sol. secundum lagam Mircenorum.
Ceorles wergild is CC and VI and LX þrymsa, þæt bið twahund scyllinga be Myrcna lage.
Wergeld eines Gemeinfreien ist 266 Tremissen (nach Dänenrecht Ld), d. i. 200 Schilling nach Mercier-Recht [3¹/₃ Pfund].
The wergild of a ceorl is 266 thrymsas (by Danish law, Ld), that is 200 shillings by Mercian law [3⅓ pounds].
A ceorl's wergild is 266 thrymsas, which is 200 shillings according to the law of the Mercians.
A commoner’s wergild is two hundred and sixty-six thrymsas, that is, two hundred shillings according to the law of the Mercians.
div.note: D reads ‘CC ⁊ LXVI’; Ld later 267 (but closer to the correct exact 266⅔). H writes ‘þþ’ (i.e. ‘þæt’ twice). Liebermann compares Mirce 1.

This is the final clause of the text’s “original” section, which likely dates from the ninth century but may have been composed as early as the mid-seventh century. The clauses that follow (nos. 7–12) are all composed by Archbishop Wulfstan.

note.seg: less archaic, a departure from the original
267 in Ld später [aber dem richtigen (genau 266²/₃) näher]
267 in Ld, later [but nearer to the correct figure (exactly 266²/₃)]
Nur beim Gemeinfreien steht in Northumbrien und Mercien das Wergeld gleich; dessen Verhältnis zum Adel aber ist bei den beiden Stämmen verschieden
Only for the common freeman is the wergild the same in Northumbria and Mercia; his relation to the nobility, however, differs between the two peoples

Emendiere (mit Kemble in Brit. rev. 1841, 71): 266⅔. Vielleicht kam der Bearbeiter von l hier ausnahmsweise durch eigene Kenntnis dem Genauen näher.—Chadwick (Anglo-Sax. inst. 77) vergleicht des Carl Wergeld 768 Pfennig in Leges inter Brettos et Scottos.—Kaum ein anderer als ein Mercier hätte den Northumbrischen Wert gerade in Mercische Währung umgerechnet; o. Einl. 4

Emend (with Kemble in Brit. rev. 1841, 71) to 266⅔. Perhaps the reviser of l here, exceptionally, came nearer to the exact figure through his own knowledge. — Chadwick (Anglo-Sax. inst. 77) compares the carl’s wergild of 768 pence in the Leges inter Brettos et Scottos. — Hardly anyone but a Mercian would have converted the Northumbrian value into Mercian currency in particular; above Introduction 4
Zufügung l's zwar sachlich richtig, aber überflüssig, da ja das ganze Stück zur Denalagu gehört
Addition by l, factually correct but superfluous, since the whole piece belongs to the Danelaw anyway
